title: Comment from Lynn Gessler
printtext:
Docket No. FDA-2015-D-4750-0439
Food and Drug Administration
5630 Fishers Lane, Room 1061
Rockville, MD 20852

Re: FDA’s Reclassification of Desiccated Thyroid Extract (DTE) as a Biologic

To Whom It May Concern:

I am writing with deep concern about the FDA’s recent decision to reclassify desiccated thyroid extract (DTE) as a biologic. For more than 100 years, DTE has been a lifeline for patients like me who do not do well on synthetic thyroid medicines. The decision puts that lifeline at risk.

For many of us, DTE isn’t just another treatment option, it’s the only treatment that makes daily life possible. Without it, we face fatigue, weight gain, brain fog, depression, and countless other symptoms that make even basic tasks difficult. I have seen how quickly quality of life deteriorates when DTE is taken away, and I am not alone.

This reclassification just doesn’t make sense for patients. It creates unnecessary barriers and opens the door for a single company to control the product, driving up costs and shutting out the compounding pharmacies that have provided access to this medicine for years. The result will be fewer choices, higher prices, and patients left with no effective alternatives.

What makes this especially painful is that this change wasn’t made because of new science or safety concerns. It seems to be happening because of pressure from a large drug company with financial interest. Patients like me are left wondering why our voices don’t matter more than corporate profits.

I urge the FDA to reconsider this harmful action. Please keep DTE regulated the same way it has been for decades, protect patient choice and access, and put patients first by ensuring DTE remains available at compounding pharmacies for when other treatments fail.

For hundreds and thousands of Americans, this is not an abstract policy change. It’s about whether we can live full, healthy lives. I ask you to stand with patients and preserve access to DTE.

Respectfully,

This reclassification threatens to eliminate an essential therapy by restricting its availability to a single manufacturer and cutting compounding pharmacies out of the supply chain. That outcome will reduce patient choice, drive up costs, and undermine the physician’s ability to exercise clinical judgment in tailoring care to the individual.

What makes this action especially troubling is that it appears to rest not on new scientific evidence or safety concerns, but rather on a change in regulatory posture that is inconsistent with FDA’s own long-standing treatment of DTE. The process was unusual, lacking the transparency and public engagement that a decision of this magnitude demands.

I urge FDA to reconsider. DTE has been prescribed safely for more than a century. It should continue to be regulated as a drug, not a biologic, and remain available through compounding pharmacies so that physicians can prescribe it when clinically appropriate. My patients’ well-being depends on it.

Respectfully,

title: Comment from Mindy Valle
printtext:
I strongly support modernizing emergency medical kits (EMKs) aboard commercial aircraft, but I urge the FAA to ensure that increased flexibility for air carriers does not result in reduced minimum standards for lifesaving medications and equipment.

As both a registered nurse and the parent of a young child with multiple severe food allergies, including allergies capable of causing anaphylaxis, I am acutely aware of how quickly a medical emergency can become life-threatening. An aircraft at cruising altitude is a uniquely vulnerable environment. Passengers cannot simply call 911 or be transported to an emergency department, and diversion to the nearest airport can take significant time. The medical resources available onboard during those critical minutes matter.

Any performance-based standard should therefore establish clear, enforceable minimum requirements for time-sensitive emergencies, particularly anaphylaxis. Commercial aircraft should carry an adequate supply of epinephrine in forms and doses appropriate for both adults and children. The availability of epinephrine should not depend upon whether an individual passenger happens to have brought an autoinjector, whether that device is accessible, or whether a medically trained passenger happens to be onboard.

I also urge the FAA to consider pediatric patients specifically when establishing minimum EMK capabilities. Children are not simply smaller adults. Medication concentrations, dosing, equipment sizes, and treatment needs can differ significantly. A kit may technically contain a medication while still being functionally inadequate if it cannot be safely administered to a child.

In addition, flexibility in kit contents should be paired with strong requirements for inspection, replacement of expired medications, accessibility during an emergency, standardized organization and labeling, and meaningful crew training. Flight crews should be able to rapidly identify and access emergency medications, and medical professionals who volunteer to assist should not lose critical time trying to determine what medications or equipment are actually available.

I encourage the FAA to adopt a performance-based approach only if it establishes a strong national safety floor. Airlines may be permitted to exceed or adapt beyond that standard, but essential lifesaving capabilities should not vary significantly depending on which carrier a passenger happens to fly.

For passengers with serious medical conditions and for parents of children at risk of anaphylaxis, adequate onboard emergency medical resources are not a convenience. At 35,000 feet, they may represent the only immediate medical treatment available. I urge the FAA to prioritize passenger safety by requiring EMKs that are adequately stocked, pediatric-capable, readily accessible, consistently maintained, and equipped to treat anaphylaxis and other foreseeable life-threatening emergencies.

Epinephrine is available for severe allergic reactions, and naloxone is available for opioid overdoses. Intranasal seizure rescue medications are compact, easy to store, and can be administered without an IV. The inability to obtain immediate medical care while in the air makes their inclusion in aircraft emergency medical kits even more important.

Epilepsy is a serious neurological disease affecting millions of people. Those living with epilepsy deserve the same access to emergency, potentially lifesaving treatment as passengers experiencing other medical emergencies.

I respectfully urge the FAA to require an appropriate seizure rescue medication in all commercial aircraft emergency medical kits and to establish clear protocols for its administration. This is a practical and potentially lifesaving change that could make air travel safer for people living with epilepsy and their families.

Recommendation – Add Return-to-Service Activity on Transport-Category Aircraft as a Qualifying Recent-Experience Activity

I recommend that the FAA expand the proposed recent-experience requirements to recognize qualifying return-to-service (RTS) activity involving transport-category aircraft.

Specifically, I recommend that completion of at least six qualifying RTS events on transport-category aircraft within the preceding twelve calendar months be accepted as an additional means of satisfying the Inspection Rating recent-experience requirement.

The current activity-based pathways do not fully reflect the maintenance environment in which many experienced A&P mechanics and IA holders work. In particular, mechanics supporting complex transport-category aircraft may exercise substantial technical, regulatory, inspection, records-review, and airworthiness responsibilities without routinely performing annual inspections or personally executing major repairs or major alterations in a manner that qualifies under the existing activity pathways.

A return-to-service event involving a transport-category aircraft may require a mechanic to evaluate completed maintenance, review applicable technical data, assess maintenance records and required documentation, verify completion of inspection requirements, evaluate open discrepancies, confirm compliance with applicable Airworthiness Directives and other airworthiness requirements, and determine whether the aircraft is eligible for approval for return to service.

These responsibilities directly exercise many of the same competencies that the Inspection Rating is intended to preserve, including regulatory knowledge, technical-data application, records review, inspection judgment, and airworthiness decision making.

Accordingly, I recommend that the FAA add a sixth qualifying recent-experience pathway based on documented RTS activity involving transport-category aircraft. Specifically, completion of at least six qualifying RTS events within the preceding twelve calendar months should satisfy the recent-experience requirement.

To ensure that the activity represents meaningful exercise of inspection and airworthiness responsibilities, the FAA could define a qualifying RTS event as one in which the Inspection Rating holder personally exercises return-to-service authority following a substantive maintenance event on a transport-category aircraft and makes the required maintenance record entry or otherwise assumes documented responsibility for the return-to-service determination.

This additional pathway would better recognize the actual work performed by experienced mechanics in corporate, business aviation, air carrier, and other complex aircraft maintenance environments while maintaining an objective, documentable, and safety-relevant recent-experience standard.

title: Comment from Tracy Ryan
printtext:
Re: Docket No. FAA–2026–6671

I strongly support the FAA's proposal to replace the current Inspection Authorization (IA) with a permanent Inspection Rating. Eliminating the recurring renewal process while retaining appropriate qualification requirements is a welcome modernization that reduces unnecessary administrative burden while maintaining aviation safety.

I respectfully request that the FAA expand the transition provisions to include mechanics whose Inspection Authorization expired before the effective date of the final rule.

Under the proposal, an individual who holds a valid Inspection Authorization on the effective date would transition directly to the new Inspection Rating. However, an equally qualified mechanic whose Inspection Authorization expired before that date would still be required to begin the process anew by submitting FAA Form 8610-1, obtaining authorization from the FAA, and successfully completing another Inspection Authorization knowledge test and oral evaluation.

This creates an arbitrary distinction based solely on the expiration date of an Inspection Authorization rather than on the mechanic's qualifications, competence, or continued involvement in aircraft maintenance.

For example, two mechanics could have identical backgrounds, identical experience, and identical employment histories. One mechanic whose IA remains valid on the effective date would automatically receive the new Inspection Rating. The other mechanic, whose IA expired only a short time earlier—even by a single day—would be required to repeat the entire application and examination process. The difference between these two individuals is not one of knowledge, skill, or safety, but simply the date on which the authorization expired.

An individual who previously earned an Inspection Authorization has already demonstrated the qualifications, knowledge, and experience required by the FAA. Many former IA holders continue to work full-time as certificated mechanics after their authorization expires. Although they are no longer authorized to perform IA-specific functions such as annual inspections or major repair and alteration approvals, they continue to maintain and develop the technical knowledge and maintenance skills that originally qualified them to hold an Inspection Authorization.

I encourage the FAA to establish a pathway that allows former IA holders whose authorization expired before the effective date of the final rule to obtain the new Inspection Rating without repeating the initial application and examination process, provided they can demonstrate that they have remained actively engaged in aircraft maintenance as certificated mechanics since their IA expired.

This approach would be fully consistent with the FAA's stated objective of reducing unnecessary administrative burden while maintaining safety. It would recognize qualifications that have already been demonstrated, avoid requiring experienced aviation maintenance professionals to repeat examinations they have previously passed, and eliminate an arbitrary distinction based solely on the effective date of the rule rather than on any meaningful difference in competency or safety.

Providing this transition pathway would also increase the number of experienced mechanics available to perform inspection functions. At a time when the aviation industry continues to face challenges in recruiting and retaining qualified maintenance personnel, enabling former IA holders who have remained active in aircraft maintenance to regain inspection privileges without unnecessary administrative barriers would strengthen the aviation maintenance workforce while preserving the FAA's high standards for safety. This outcome would benefit aircraft owners, repair stations, and the general aviation community by expanding the pool of experienced inspection-qualified mechanics without reducing qualification standards.

Thank you for considering this recommendation.

title: Comment from Shaune Maycock
printtext:
I am an FAA-certificated Airframe and Powerplant mechanic who has held an Inspection Authorization (IA) for 17 years and has owned and operated an aircraft maintenance facility for the past 20 years. During that time, I have performed hundreds of annual inspections, major repairs, and major alterations on a wide variety of general aviation aircraft.

Overall, I support replacing the current Inspection Authorization with an Inspection Rating. The proposal reduces unnecessary administrative burden while maintaining the high standards expected of mechanics exercising inspection privileges.

My support is based on the understanding that this change will not result in additional testing or certification requirements for mechanics to demonstrate proficiency on specific aircraft types, makes, or models. Current regulations already require mechanics to determine whether they possess the knowledge, experience, and current technical data necessary to perform maintenance or inspections on a particular aircraft. That principle has served the industry well and should remain unchanged.

I encourage the FAA to consider one additional aspect that directly affects aviation safety.

A complete annual inspection is physically demanding. It often requires climbing ladders, crawling beneath instrument panels, accessing wing roots, landing gear compartments, tail cones, and other confined areas. If a mechanic cannot physically access these areas, it becomes difficult to ensure every required inspection item has been completed.

During my 17 years as an IA, I have attended FAA-sponsored IA seminars. I have tremendous respect for the experienced mechanics recognized for decades of service. However, I have also observed some individuals whose physical limitations raised legitimate questions about whether they could still perform every aspect of a complete annual inspection.

My concern is not age. Many mechanics remain highly capable well beyond traditional retirement age, while others develop physical limitations much earlier. My concern is whether an individual exercising the privileges of an Inspection Rating remains physically capable of performing the duties required by the regulations.

I encourage the FAA to consider implementing a process for periodically observing the physical ability of Inspection Rating holders to perform those duties. One possible approach would be an observation by an Aviation Safety Inspector at the local FSDO, or another FAA-approved evaluation process. The purpose would not be to re-test technical knowledge, but simply to determine whether the mechanic can physically perform the inspection tasks associated with the privileges of the Inspection Rating. Any additional evaluation should be based on demonstrated functional ability rather than age alone.

Finally, I would like to raise a broader concern regarding mechanic certification and recent experience requirements. While this proposal focuses on Inspection Rating holders, I believe the FAA should also place greater emphasis on enforcing the recent experience requirements that already apply to certificated Airframe and Powerplant mechanics.
As the owner of an aircraft maintenance facility for 20 years, I have interviewed applicants who held valid A&P certificates but had spent little or no time actively working in aircraft maintenance. Some obtained their certificate primarily to maintain their own aircraft. There is nothing improper about that; however, they are still required to meet the recent experience requirements before exercising the privileges of their certificate.

In my experience, the issue is not a lack of regulation but a lack of enforcement. Mechanics who actively work in the industry every day are expected to remain current, while others who perform only occasional maintenance may continue exercising certificate privileges despite not meeting the recency requirements. Consistent enforcement of the existing regulations would promote a more uniform professional standard and further enhance aviation safety.

I appreciate the FAA's efforts to modernize the Inspection Authorization process while maintaining safety. I believe this proposal is a positive step forward and encourage the FAA to continue improving safety without creating unnecessary burdens for certificated mechanics.

However, I recommend that the FAA further clarify the proposed rolling twelve-calendar-month recent-experience requirements, provide nationally consistent guidance regarding the meaning of “actively engaged,” reconsider whether the fixed-base-of-operations requirement remains appropriate in today’s digital and mobile maintenance environment, and clearly define acceptable documentation for demonstrating recent experience.

I also recommend that the FAA reconsider whether the proposed Inspection Rating Airman Certification Standards (ACS) framework is the most appropriate testing model for the IR. While I support clear, standardized, and legally enforceable testing standards, the FAA should demonstrate why integrating task-specific risk-management elements into the Inspection Rating standard is necessary and how those elements will be objectively evaluated. The FAA should consider whether a more focused PTS-style standard would better evaluate the technical, regulatory, records, inspection, and airworthiness competencies central to IR privileges.

Finally, I recommend careful review of the optional oral-examination pathways for maintaining or restoring recent experience. A lapse in recent experience should not, by itself, be treated as evidence that an otherwise qualified mechanic is no longer competent to hold the rating. Any oral examination process should be objective, nationally consistent, narrowly tailored to current inspection knowledge, and governed by clear standards regarding scope, scoring, retesting, and potential consequences.

title: Comment from JOHN MCDERMOTT

I am writing as a current Inspection Authorization (IA) holder to comment on the proposed conversion of the IA to a permanent Inspection Rating (IR) with a rolling recent-experience requirement. I support eliminating the biennial March renewal process and the “start-over” consequence of an expired IA. A non-expiring rating with a 12-month recent-experience requirement is a practical modernization that reduces administrative burden while preserving safety.
Proficiency and Recent Experience; The five activity options from § 65.93(a) remain appropriate. The strongest safety path is actual exercise of the privileges—performing annual inspections or major repairs/alterations requiring IA/IR approval. Progressive inspections are also valuable when applicable.
The 8-hour refresher course and FAA oral test should remain available as alternatives. The final rule and guidance should:
Emphasize hands-on exercise of privileges as the preferred method of maintaining proficiency.
Explicitly confirm that courses and seminars listed on the FAA Safety Team (FAASTeam) website (FAASafety.gov), including those that also qualify for AMT Awards Program credit, continue to satisfy the 8-hour refresher option.
Provide clear examples of acceptable documentation for each of the five options.
Confirm that records need only be retained for the preceding 24 months and produced upon request, with no new mandatory reporting outside of surveillance or investigation.
Clarify that completion of an acceptable 8-hour course or oral test restores privileges for the next 12 months without re-application or a written exam.
The proposed 24-month transition window plus grace period is reasonable, provided the process to obtain a replacement mechanic certificate showing the Inspection Rating is simple, online, and free of charge.
Recommendation; Adopt the permanent Inspection Rating and rolling 12-month recent-experience structure essentially as proposed. Strengthen the guidance to prioritize actual exercise of inspection privileges, retain the established FAASTeam/AMT Awards pathway for refresher credit, and provide clear, low-burden documentation methods. This maintains safety, reduces unnecessary administrative work, and gives IA/IR holders a practical path to remain current.

title: Comment from Michael Moore
printtext:
I agree that putting the IR on the certificate eliminates an additional cert, but I oppose the proposed replacement of the Inspection Authorization with a permanent Inspection Rating that relies principally upon self-maintained records of recent experience. This will not go well and this is my short answer.

Inspection Authorization privileges are granted based upon two essential qualifications: a thorough working knowledge of the applicable regulations and maintenance standards, and substantial relevant experience within the aviation-maintenance industry. The written examination may adequately establish an applicant’s knowledge at original issuance, but an examination taken once cannot establish professional currency indefinitely. Only continued relevant experience, recurrent exposure to changing regulations and maintenance information, and meaningful oversight can establish that an individual remains qualified to exercise these privileges.

I also disagree with issuing or preserving inspection privileges as what are sometimes informally called “trophy certificates.” By that term, I mean credentials sought or retained primarily for status by individuals who are not genuinely and actively engaged in the work upon which the privileges are based. Active engagement is not an incidental qualification. It is an express basis for initial issuance under § 65.91 and continued renewal under § 65.93. A person who wants the credential but does not maintain meaningful participation in certificated-aircraft maintenance does not satisfy the purpose of these requirements.

Fraud, abuse, and falsification already occur within the aviation-maintenance system. This includes applicants misrepresenting their qualifications or experience and authorization holders documenting work, inspections, or approvals for which they were not properly qualified or which they did not properly perform. The existence of falsification regulations and FAA enforcement actions demonstrates that self-certification cannot always be accepted without verification. The FAA should examine and disclose its own enforcement data concerning fraudulent experience claims, falsified maintenance records, improper annual inspections, and unauthorized approvals before concluding that less frequent oversight will provide an equivalent level of safety.

A rule that eliminates scheduled renewal and substitutes self-maintained records risks allowing unqualified or inactive individuals to retain inspection privileges largely unchecked. It also makes enforcement primarily reactive: the FAA may discover noncompliance only after defective work, an improper approval for return to service, an enforcement investigation, or an accident has brought the individual’s records under scrutiny. Oversight is most valuable when it identifies a deficiency before that deficiency contributes to an unsafe condition.

This proposal would also largely erase the practical distinction between ordinary mechanic privileges and the substantially greater authority exercised by an IA. An IA does not merely perform maintenance. An IA independently determines whether an aircraft conforms to its approved configuration and is in a condition for safe operation following an annual inspection and may approve aircraft and related products for return to service following major repairs and major alterations. These are consequential airworthiness determinations and justify a higher continuing standard.

Other airman privileges are routinely conditioned upon continuing demonstrations of fitness or currency. Depending upon the operation and privileges exercised, pilots may be subject to medical qualification, recurrent training, flight reviews, recent-flight-experience requirements, proficiency checks, and drug-and-alcohol testing requirements. Although those requirements differ according to the operation, the underlying safety principle is consistent: holding a certificate or rating does not, by itself, establish continuing qualification to exercise every privilege indefinitely.

Inspection personnel should not be treated differently merely because the FAA seeks to reduce its administrative workload. Administrative efficiency is a legitimate objective, but it is not sufficient justification for removing the only routine external verification that an IA holder remains active, properly equipped, informed, and professionally current.

A better approach would retain periodic FAA renewal while modernizing the process. Renewal could be handled electronically through IACRA, supported by documented qualifying activity and mandatory recurrent training. The FAA could also conduct targeted or random audits of renewal activity, facilities, technical-data access, and inspection records. This would reduce administrative burden while preserving meaningful oversight and deterring inactive, unqualified, or dishonest applicants from obtaining or retaining inspection privileges.

title: Comment from Thomas Soerens
printtext:
Docket No.: FAA-2026-6671-0001
Mechanic Certification: Inspection Rating and Recent Experience Requirements

Regarding the NPRM to add an IR rating to the A&P Airman Certificate, I am opposed to the proposed regulatory changes. In my opinion – the NPRM is ‘working too hard for what little you want to accomplish.’ The primary ‘little’ you want to accomplish is to remove the FAA ASI’s responsibility to review and process the Application Form 8610-1 (Application) and Form 8610-5 (IA card) bi-annually. I have been an IA since 1975. I have completed a lot of renewal forms.

14 CFR 65.91(a) states: An application for an inspection authorization is made on a form and in a manner prescribed by the Administrator.

The form and manner for the past 70 years, the Inspection Authorization Renewal has been a paper application and card for the IA authorization.

The term ‘Form and Manner’ indicates FAA Guidance is the process, meaning no NPRM is necessary to make changes. Eliminating the FSDO ASI review of Form 8610-1 and the issue of the bi-annual renewal letter can be accomplished in the IACRA System without having ASI ‘hands on.’ The only element currently missing in IACRA is the issuing of the renewal authorization letter.

Possibly 90% of IA renewal is already in place. This electronic system could be upgraded to include the renewal letter function. The Volpe Center in Cambridge, Ma or whomever has the IACRA contract could assist in this upgrade – and any added ‘feature’ deemed necessary by the FSDO (i.e. Form and Manner Guidance – no NPRM needed).

I am a DAR-T. Annually, in DMS (Designee Management System) I electronically answer a list of questions, digitally sign the application stating the information is true and correct and SUBMIT the application. DMS processes my request at that submission, and if all my answers are correct – it generates my renewal letter with the submission date, the new expiration date of my designation, and the Letter of Authority, signed by my FSDO’s Front Line Manager. The ASI (Managing Specialist) does not review or issue any part of that designation renewal.

IACRA could be developed to function in the same capacity for Inspection Authorization renewal, and no ASI would be involved in the renewal process. IACRA has link to NVIS in the event the FSDO/IFO decides to review an application – if the ASI determines that IA may require dedicated oversight.

Currently IACRA makes a determination if you have the correct minimum number of Annual Inspections, Progressive Inspections, or Major Repairs/Alteration for renewal. IACRA also has the requirement for listing the approved training course name and number and uploading that document and/or an Activity Report. IACRA allows only one renewal method per application (ex. Sufficient annual inspections or training, but not both) before the system moves to the next phase.

Within the 94 pages of the NPRM – there was no discussion of safety concerns with the current IA Regulations and renewal process – other than the review of IA paperwork is ‘work’ for the ASI. For 70 years the current regulations have existed. The NPRM (III Background, B. Need for Rulemaking Action, Paragraph 1, .pdf page 13) states there has been no substantive review of the IA rules for almost 3 decades. The ‘system must have been working effectively for not requiring a review for that long of period. The NPRM paragraph (second sentence) also states in part: ‘Since that time, FAA and industry have enjoyed advances in technology and processes, - - - “

If the NPRM ‘believes’ that text – then use and enhance the existing IACRA system as the advance in technology and processes. Please do not change the Regulations just for the sake of change. The NPRM, in my opinion, opens too many doors for the FAA to lose accountably of an IA’s currency, which could result in illegal entries for return to service.

Additionally, for an IA @$56.45/hr to attend an 8-hour training session is $56.45 x 8hr = $451.60. Added costs for lost revenue of the base of operations when the IA attends that training (lead shop floor technician is ½ of the shop rate) which is $112 x 8hr = $896.00, has a cost of $1348.00 per year, ($2696.00 per 2-years). This cost does not change for an IA in this NPRM. Training is still required.

The NPRM figure of $14.11 to complete the renewal form every 2 years – is really an insignificant cost (.5% of the training cost) per IA.

Thank you for your consideration of my comments. Please read the IACRA User Guide for IA Renewal as an element of your evaluation.

title: Comment from CAE
printtext:
To Whom It May Concern:
I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the FAA's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking regarding the replacement of the Inspection Authorization (IA) with an Inspection Rating and the transition to rolling recent-experience requirements.
I support the FAA's proposal to streamline the maintenance of inspection privileges and align the Inspection Rating with other mechanic ratings. Reducing administrative burden while maintaining safety and competency standards represents a positive modernization of the certification framework. [ACTION NEE...Deadlines | Outlook], [IA Renewal...iderartion | Outlook]
As the FAA considers the future structure of inspection-rating qualifications and recent-experience requirements, I respectfully encourage consideration of maintenance human factors and inspection-supervision competencies as activities that directly support the safe exercise of inspection privileges.
The holder of an Inspection Authorization, and under the proposed rule an Inspection Rating, is authorized not only to perform inspections but also to supervise progressive inspections. The supervisory component of this privilege is significant. Effective inspection supervision requires communication of inspection requirements, coordination of maintenance personnel, evaluation of discrepancies, oversight of corrective actions, review of documentation, and communication of airworthiness-related decisions. These activities directly affect inspection quality, regulatory compliance, and aviation safety. [RE: IA ren...training - | Outlook], [RE: IA ren...rotection | Outlook]
The aviation maintenance community has long recognized that human factors are among the most significant contributors to maintenance errors. Communication failures, ineffective supervision, poor coordination, documentation deficiencies, and decision-making errors can directly influence airworthiness outcomes. As a result, training that addresses these subjects should not necessarily be viewed as general professional development but rather as maintenance-safety competencies that support the effective performance of inspection responsibilities.
I encourage the FAA to consider recognizing instruction related to:

Maintenance human factors;
Inspection-team communication;
Maintenance documentation and record accuracy;
Supervisory oversight of inspection activities;
Error prevention and error-management strategies;
Airworthiness decision-making;
Risk management in maintenance environments; and
Inspection-related safety culture.

Such training directly supports the competencies required to exercise inspection privileges safely and effectively. These topics strengthen the ability of inspection-rating holders to prevent maintenance errors, ensure regulatory compliance, improve documentation quality, and supervise inspection activities in accordance with FAA standards.
As the FAA moves toward a recent-experience-based model, I believe consideration should be given to recognizing certain human-factors and inspection-supervision training activities as qualifying means of maintaining inspection competency, provided the curriculum is directly linked to aircraft maintenance, inspection practices, airworthiness determinations, and regulatory compliance.
I commend the FAA for pursuing a modernization effort that reduces administrative burden while maintaining safety oversight. Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments for consideration.
Respectfully,

printtext:
Subject: Comments on NPRM FAA-2026-6671 – Mechanic Certification: Inspection Rating and Recent Experience Requirements
I support the FAA's objective of reducing unnecessary administrative workload associated with Inspection Authorization renewals. Redirecting Aviation Safety Inspector resources from processing renewal applications toward meaningful surveillance and safety oversight is a worthwhile goal.
However, I respectfully recommend that the FAA modify the proposal to include a mechanism for periodic independent verification of a mechanic's recent-experience qualifications.
Under the proposed rule, Inspection Rating holders would maintain qualification records independently without any routine validation by the FAA. This represents a significant change from the current IA renewal process, where an FAA inspector periodically verifies that renewal requirements have been satisfied.
Although the proposal appropriately maintains recent-experience requirements, it appears to rely almost exclusively on self-determination of currency until an FAA inspection, investigation, or enforcement action occurs.
I recommend the FAA consider implementing a simple electronic validation process, perhaps every two years, allowing Inspection Rating holders to upload documentation through an online FAA portal. Such a process could be largely automated, would eliminate the administrative burden associated with current paper renewals, and would preserve an important element of independent oversight.
This modification would satisfy the FAA's stated objective of reducing paperwork while maintaining confidence that mechanics exercising Inspection Rating privileges continue to meet qualification requirements.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment.
Mike (RotorDoc) Broderick, Contributing Writer for Helicopter Maintenance Magazine

title: Comment from Joshua Rauch
printtext:
I support the FAA’s proposal to replace the current Inspection Authorization (IA) with an Inspection Rating (IR) and to transition from a periodic renewal process to a recent-experience-based system.

The proposed Inspection Rating more accurately reflects how experienced maintenance professionals remain engaged in aircraft maintenance and airworthiness oversight throughout their careers. I believe this approach will reduce administrative burden while maintaining or improving aviation safety.

I recommend that the FAA explicitly clarify in the final rule that qualifying recent experience may include maintenance, inspection, supervisory, quality assurance, and technical oversight duties performed under a Part 145 Repair Station certificate.

Many experienced mechanics holding inspection privileges serve in positions such as inspectors, avionics specialists, quality assurance personnel, maintenance supervisors, shop managers, directors of maintenance, and technical leaders. These individuals routinely exercise maintenance judgment, oversee maintenance activities, evaluate airworthiness, review maintenance records, supervise corrective actions, and ensure regulatory compliance, even when they do not personally perform a significant number of annual inspections or approve major repairs and alterations each year.

Without explicit recognition of these duties, the final rule could unintentionally discourage experienced maintenance professionals from accepting supervisory or specialized technical positions while still remaining actively engaged in aircraft maintenance.

I recommend the FAA clarify that employment and maintenance-related duties performed under a certificated Part 145 Repair Station, including supervisory and inspection-related responsibilities, constitute qualifying recent experience for the purpose of maintaining Inspection Rating currency.

Such clarification would better reflect the structure of modern maintenance organizations while preserving the intent of ensuring that Inspection Rating holders remain actively involved in aviation maintenance and airworthiness activities.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Respectfully,

title: Comment from MARK BINGAMON
printtext:
To Whom It May Concern,

I support the FAA's proposal to replace the Inspection Authorization with an Inspection Rating and to streamline the process for maintaining inspection privileges. The proposed shift toward recent-experience requirements appears to reduce administrative burden while maintaining safety oversight.

I submit this comment as an aviation professional who has managed aircraft maintenance and refurbishment projects for many years. While I am not an A&P mechanic or Inspection Authorization holder, I have worked closely with maintenance teams, inspectors, planners, and customers in large maintenance environments.

During my career, I have observed that some of the most costly maintenance and inspection issues did not result from a lack of technical skill. Instead, they resulted from human factors such as communication, coordination, documentation review, and decision-making.

For example, I witnessed multiple situations where communication breakdowns between departments resulted in required parts not being ordered. The maintenance requirements were known, but the information was not effectively communicated. As a result, aircraft deliveries were delayed while waiting for parts to arrive.

In another project, maintenance personnel began disassembling portions of an aircraft to accomplish a service bulletin. Only after significant labor had been expended was it discovered that the service bulletin was not applicable due to a previously installed aircraft modification. The technical work itself was performed correctly, but a more thorough review of aircraft records and configuration information beforehand could have prevented unnecessary labor, parts procurement, and restocking costs.

These experiences reinforced my belief that maintenance human factors including communication, documentation review, coordination, supervision, and decision-making have a direct impact on inspection effectiveness, maintenance quality, regulatory compliance, and aviation safety.

As the FAA develops the framework for Inspection Ratings and recent-experience requirements, I encourage consideration of maintenance human factors, inspection supervision, documentation quality, and airworthiness decision-making as competencies that directly support the safe exercise of inspection privileges. These topics are not simply professional-development subjects, they are practical tools that help prevent maintenance errors and improve inspection outcomes.

Thank you for considering these comments.
Respectfully,
Concerned Aviator

title: Comment from Brian Johnson
printtext:
I am a certificated Airframe and Powerplant mechanic with a current Inspection Authorization and 36 years of aviation maintenance experience. I am writing in strong support of the FAA's proposal to replace the Inspection Authorization with an Inspection Rating on the mechanic certificate.

The current biennial renewal system creates administrative burden without meaningfully measuring competency or currency. Replacing it with a permanent rating — consistent with how Airframe and Powerplant ratings already work — is a logical, overdue improvement. The shift to rolling recent experience requirements also makes far more sense than an arbitrary renewal deadline tied to odd-numbered years.

I support this rule. I ask for one amendment before it is finalized.

The recent experience activities proposed under § 65.93(a) do not include aviation maintenance supervisory and management roles. This is a significant gap. Many of the most experienced IA holders in the industry have moved into roles as Directors of Maintenance, Quality Assurance Managers, and Maintenance Supervisors. These professionals oversee inspection programs, manage A&P teams, ensure regulatory compliance, and maintain airworthiness daily. They are unquestionably "actively engaged" in aviation maintenance — yet nothing in the proposed rule explicitly recognizes their experience as qualifying.

Excluding supervisory and management roles risks sidelining the most experienced segment of our workforce at a time when the aviation industry is already facing a serious experience and staffing shortage. It would be counterproductive to a rule that is otherwise designed to reduce burden and retain qualified professionals.

I urge the FAA to explicitly include aviation maintenance supervisory and management roles as qualifying recent experience activities under § 65.93(a). This single addition would make an already strong proposal significantly better.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.
